answer: Hypothesis: In the NLSY79 data, the racial difference in BA-track educational progress is a function of socioeconomic status, not a uniform Black advantage. As of 1979 (respondents aged 14–22), Black students do NOT have an overall advantage in college progress: only 3.6% had completed ≥14 grades (2+ years of college) vs 7.4% of non-Black/non-Hispanic students (Hispanic 3.9%). The observed Black–non-Black gap is concentrated at low family income: descriptively, 2.7% of low-SES Black students had reached ≥14 grades vs 12.0% of low-SES non-Black students (≈9.3 pp gap), while at mid-SES the gap shrinks to 3.4% vs 4.7% (1.3 pp) and at high-SES it disappears entirely (6.3% vs 6.7%). After controlling for age, sex and family size, the race×SES interaction is statistically significant (Black×Mid OR 3.95 [1.86, 8.40]; Black×High OR 3.11 [1.47, 6.60] vs the low-SES baseline), and the cell-specific ORs for Black vs same-SES non-Black/non-Hispanic students are: Low SES OR 0.30 [0.17, 0.53], Mid SES OR 1.19 [0.72, 2.0] (n.s.), High SES OR 0.94 [0.57, 1.55] (n.s.). Hispanic students show the same pattern (Low OR 0.44 [0.30, 0.63]; Mid OR 0.94 [0.58, 1.52]; High OR 1.21 [0.78, 1.88]). Therefore: the socioeconomic gradient is the primary driver of the racial gap in BA-track progress — among low-SES students Black students are about 70% less likely to be on the BA track, but once family income reaches mid or high levels, Black and non-Black students progress at statistically indistinguishable rates. Any "advantage" attributable to race per se is not supported; SES explains the within-group divergence.

As of 1979 (ages 14-22), Black students show no overall advantage: 3.6% had completed >=14 grades (2+ years of college) vs 7.4% of non-Black/non-Hispanic students. The Black-non-Black gap is concentrated at low family income (2.7% vs 12.0%; adjusted OR 0.30, 95% CI 0.17-0.53), shrinks at mid income (3.4% vs 4.7%; OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.72-1.98, n.s.) and disappears at high income (6.3% vs 6.7%; OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.57-1.55, n.s.); the Hispanic pattern is identical (Low OR 0.44, Mid 0.94, High 1.21, the latter two n.s.). payload.workflow: 1) Inspection of data/nls_raw.csv (N=12,686 x 61 cols). IMPORTANT: there is NO real BA-completion variable and no post-1979 education waves; the outcome is a proxy — educational progress as of 1979 when respondents were 14-22 years old ('Highest grade completed, 1979' >= 14 = 2+ years of college; code 95 treated as missing). 2) SES constructed (no pre-categorized SES exists): terciles of log1p(total net family income, previous calendar year 1978, recorded 1979) — the most complete pre-outcome measure (80.4% non-missing); income top-coded at 75,001 retained. 3) ASVAB composite (mean of 4 sections) was NOT a real z-score (raw mean ~476, SD ~91) so we standardized it ourselves, z=(x-mean)/sd; because it was measured in 1981 (after the 1979 outcome) it was excluded from primary models and used only as an exploratory sensitivity control. 4) Descriptive cross-tabs of the outcome by race x SES tertile with Wilson 95% CIs. 5) Logistic regressions: M1 race only, M2 +SES, M3 +SES+age+sex+family size (primary), M4 race x SES interaction with cell-specific ORs (vs same-SES non-Black/non-Hispanic reference) with Wald-based 95% CIs. 6) Sensitivity: outcomes >=13 and >=16; SES from 1985 income and 1985 wealth; ASVAB-adjusted model. Analysis sample n=10,071 (listwise: grade + 1979 income available); income missingness is mildly differential by race (Black 17.4% vs Non-Black 20.1%).
